entries.name: Wiktionary es→en (Yomitan build)
entries.html:
picar

  1. Grammar
    picar (first-person singular present pico, first-person singular preterite piqué, past participle picado)
    Etymology
    From pico (“beak, point”), or maybe from Latin pīcus (“woodpecker”), through a Vulgar Latin *pīccāre (“to sting, strike”). Compare English pique, French piquer, and Portuguese picar.
    1. vi
      to itch (to feel itchy; to feel a need to be scratched)
      1 example
      una tela que pica
      an itchy fabric
    2. to sting
    3. to chop
      1 example
      picar cebollas
      to chop onions
    4. to bite
    5. cook
      to mince, to dice
    6. to stab; to wound
    7. col
      to snack; to nibble; to have a bite
      1 example
      me apetece picar algo
      I fancy a bite to eat
    8. to rot; to decay; to eat away; to rust
    9. to pique
    10. to crush (ice)
    11. vi
      to sting or be pungent to the lips or tongue, be spicy or, of a candy, very sour
      1 example
      Este chile pica mucho.
      Th is chili is very hot .
    12. 🇲🇽 sl
      to sexually penetrate, fuck
    13. vr
      to get angry, get annoyed, take offence
    14. vr
      to turn sour
    15. vr 🇲🇽
      to get addicted, fascinated, enraptured
    16. vi
      to bounce
    17. to click (such as with a computer mouse)
    18. to knock (on a door)
    19. sl
      to steal, rob
      1 example
      Aprovecha y pícate algo, socio.
      Take advantage and steal something, mate.
    20. to wink (blink with only one eye as a message, signal, or suggestion)
    Wiktionary | Kaikki

entries.name: Wiktionary ru→en (Yomitan build)
entries.html:
дом

  1. Grammar
    дом • (dom) m inan (genitive до́ма, nominative plural дома́ or до́мы^*, genitive plural домо́в, relational adjective дома́шний or домово́й or домо́вый, diminutive до́мик or домо́к or дому́шка, augmentative доми́ще or доми́на, pejorative доми́шко)
    Etymology
    Inherited from Old East Slavic домъ (domŭ, “house; home”), from Proto-Slavic *dȍmъ (“house; home”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *damús, from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm (“home; house”)
    1. house, building (a residential building)
      3 examples
      обы́скивать дом за до́мом
      to search house by house
      кварти́рный дом
      apartment building ; block of flats
      Дом име́л тот немно́го неве́рный вид, како́й быва́ет, когда́ там, внутри́, спят лю́ди.
      The house had that slightly uncertain look that can happen when there are people sleeping inside.
    2. house, home (as part of a name of an establishment)
      3 examples
      изда́тельский дом
      publishing house
      сумасше́дший дом / дур до́м
      insane asylum ; mad house
      дом о́тдыха
      holiday resort
    3. plot (in some street addresses: a group of buildings sharing the same street number)
      1 example
      Моско́вское шоссе́, дом 123, ко́рпус 2, кварти́ра 10
      123 Moskovskoye highway, building 2, apartment 10
    4. home
      2 examples
      родно́й дом
      native home
      Дом англича́нина — его́ кре́пость.
      An Englishman's home is his castle.
    5. dynasty, noble house
      2 examples
      дом Рома́новых
      the Romanov dynasty
      чума́ на о́ба ва́ши до́ма
      a plague on both your houses
    Wiktionary | Kaikki
